summary.text: Factorials are decomposed into powers of \(p\), smaller factorials, and blocks of factors prime to \(p\); truncated product expansions modulo \(p^{3r}\), together with reflection and the vanishing of the relevant reciprocal and reciprocal-square sums, show that these blocks have the required periodicity. For odd indices, the Gamma duplication formula converts the ratio to ordinary factorials, and a half-block square identity—whose sign is fixed modulo \(p\) using Fermat’s theorem—supplies the corresponding block cancellation.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(n)=\frac{\Gamma(9n+1)\Gamma(2n+1)\Gamma(3n/2+1)}
{\Gamma(9n/2+1)\Gamma(4n+1)\Gamma(3n+1)\Gamma(n+1)}.
\]
We prove the asserted congruence under the stated hypothesis that every value \(a(n)\) is an integer.

Fix a prime \(p\ge 5\). For an integer \(N\ge 0\), define the \(p\)-free block
\[
U(N)=\prod_{\substack{0\le k<N\\p\nmid k}}k.
\]
The condition \(p\nmid k\) automatically excludes \(k=0\), so this is a product of positive integers. When working modulo a power of \(p\), every factor in \(U(N)\) is a unit.

We first establish the block congruences needed later.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Harmonic sums and translated full blocks
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Fix \(r>0\), put
\[
P=p^r,
\]
and work, unless otherwise indicated, in the ring
\[
R=\mathbb Z/P^3\mathbb Z.
\]
In this ring \(P^3=0\). The elements \(2\) and \(3\) are units because \(p\ge5\).

We use the elementary truncated product formula
\[
\prod_{i\in S}(1+t f_i)
=1+t\sum_{i\in S}f_i+
\frac{t^2}{2}\left(\left(\sum_{i\in S}f_i\right)^2-
\sum_{i\in S}f_i^2\right)
\tag{1}
\]
whenever \(t^3=0\). This follows by expanding the product: every term of degree at least three in \(t\) vanishes, and
\[
\sum_{i<j}f_if_j= rac12\left(\left(\sum_i f_i\right)^2-\sum_i f_i^2\right).
\]
Two consequences will be used repeatedly:

* if \(t\sum f_i=0\) and \(t^2\sum f_i^2=0\), then
  \[
  \prod_i(1+t f_i)=1;
  \tag{2}
  \]
* if only \(t^2\sum f_i^2=0\), then comparison of (1) for \(t\) and for \(2t\) gives
  \[
  \prod_i(1+2t f_i)=\left(\prod_i(1+t f_i)\right)^2.
  \tag{3}
  \]

We now prove the required harmonic-sum vanishings. Modulo \(P\), the integers \(1\le k<P\) with \(p\nmid k\) form precisely the group \((\mathbb Z/P\mathbb Z)^\times\). Hence
\[
\sum_{\substack{0<k<P\\p\nmid k}}k^{-2}
=\sum_{u\in(\mathbb Z/P\mathbb Z)^\times}u^{-2}.
\]
Multiplication by \(2\) permutes this unit group. Therefore the sum \(S_2=\sum u^2\) satisfies \(S_2=4S_2\), and hence \(3S_2=0\). Since \(3\) is a unit, \(S_2=0\). Inversion also permutes the unit group, so
\[
\sum_{\substack{0<k<P\\p\nmid k}}k^{-2}=0\pmod P.
\tag{4}
\]
Breaking any interval of length \(cP\) into \(c\) blocks of length \(P\) gives, because translation by \(P\) does not change residues modulo \(P\),
\[
\sum_{\substack{0<k<cP\\p\nmid k}}k^{-2}=0\pmod P.
\tag{5}
\]
Consequently, after regarding the inverses in \(R\),
\[
P^2\sum_{\substack{0<k<cP\\p\nmid k}}k^{-2}=0\pmod{P^3}.
\tag{6}
\]
Indeed, (5) says that the sum is divisible by \(P\), and multiplication by \(P^2\) makes it divisible by \(P^3\).

We also need the first harmonic sum over one full block. For \(0<k<P\), set \(x=k\), \(y=P-k\). In \(R\), both are units and \(x+y=P\). A direct calculation gives
\[
P(x^{-1}+y^{-1})+P^2x^{-2}=0.
\tag{7}
\]
To see this, first
\[
x^{-1}+y^{-1}=(x+y)x^{-1}y^{-1}=P x^{-1}y^{-1}.
\]
Substitution transforms the left side of (7) into
\[
P^2x^{-1}(x^{-1}+y^{-1})=P^3x^{-2}y^{-1}=0.
\]
Sum (7) over all \(k\) with \(0<k<P\) and \(p\nmid k\). Reflection \(k\mapsto P-k\) permutes this set, so the two inverse sums occurring in the first term are equal. Thus
\[
2P\sum_{\substack{0<k<P\\p\nmid k}}k^{-1}
+P^2\sum_{\substack{0<k<P\\p\nmid k}}k^{-2}=0.
\]
The second term vanishes by (6), and \(2\) is a unit. Hence
\[
P\sum_{\substack{0<k<P\\p\nmid k}}k^{-1}=0\pmod{P^3}.
\tag{8}
\]

We can now show that a full \(P\)-block is unchanged by translation through a multiple of \(P\). For \(c\ge0\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
\prod_{\substack{0<k<P\\p\nmid k}}(cP+k)
&=U(P)\prod_{\substack{0<k<P\\p\nmid k}}(1+cP/k).
\end{aligned}
\]
Apply (2) with \(t=cP\) and \(f_k=k^{-1}\). We have \(t^3=0\), the first-order term vanishes by (8), and the second-order reciprocal-square term vanishes by (6). Therefore
\[
\prod_{\substack{0<k<P\\p\nmid k}}(cP+k)=U(P)\pmod{P^3}.
\tag{9}
\]
Splitting \([0,cP)\) into \(c\) successive blocks of length \(P\) now yields the fundamental full-block congruence
\[
U(cP)=U(P)^c\pmod{P^3}.
\tag{10}
\]
Modulo \(p\), the analogous and simpler periodicity statement is
\[
U(cp)=U(p)^c\pmod p.
\tag{11}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. The half-block identity
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Suppose that \(N=cP\) is odd. Set
\[
S=\{k:0<k<N/2+1,\ p\nmid k\},\qquad M=|S|,
\]
and write
\[
H=U(N/2+1),\qquad B=U(N).
\]
Thus \(H=\prod_{k\in S}k\). We prove
\[
H^2\,16^M=(-1)^M B\pmod{P^3}.
\tag{12}
\]

Because \(N\) is odd and divisible by \(p\), reflection \(k\mapsto N-k\) identifies the lower half \(S\) with the upper half of the \(p\)-free integers below \(N\). Put
\[
t=-N/2\in R,
\qquad
V=\prod_{k\in S}(1+t/k),
\]
where division by \(2\) is legitimate in \(R\). Since \(N=cP\), we have \(t^3=0\). Moreover, the reciprocal-square sum over the lower half vanishes after multiplication by \(P^2\). Indeed, the reciprocal-square sum over all \(0<k<N\), \(p\nmid k\), vanishes modulo \(P\) by (5); reflection sends \((N-k)^{-2}\) to \((-k)^{-2}=k^{-2}\) modulo \(P\). The full sum is therefore twice the lower-half sum, and \(2\) is invertible. It follows that
\[
t^2\sum_{k\in S}k^{-2}=0\quad\text{in }R.
\tag{13}
\]
Since \(2t=-N\), formula (3) gives
\[
\prod_{k\in S}(1-N/k)=V^2.
\tag{14}
\]

We calculate \(B\) in two ways. First, split the factors into the lower half and its reflection:
\[
\begin{aligned}
B
&=\prod_{k\in S}k\prod_{k\in S}(N-k)\\
&=H\prod_{k\in S}\bigl(-k(1-N/k)\bigr)\\
&=(-1)^M H^2V^2.
\end{aligned}
\tag{15}
\]

Second, split the \(p\)-free factors below \(N\) according to parity. Since \(p\ne2\), the even factors are exactly \(2k\) with \(k\in S\), and the odd factors are exactly \(N-2k\) with \(k\in S\). Also
\[
N-2k=-2(k-N/2)=-2k(1+t/k).
\]
Consequently
\[
\begin{aligned}
B
&=\prod_{k\in S}(2k)\prod_{k\in S}(N-2k)\\
&=(-1)^M4^M H^2V.
\end{aligned}
\tag{16}
\]
Every block appearing here is a unit in \(R\). Equations (15) and (16) therefore permit cancellation and imply \(V=4^M\). Substituting this into (15), and using \(((-1)^M)^2=1\), gives exactly
\[
H^2 16^M=(-1)^M B,
\]
which proves (12).

We record the size of the half-block. If \(p\) and \(m\) are odd, then
\[
\left|\{k:0<k<mp/2+1,\ p\nmid k\}\right|=m\lfloor p/2\rfloor.
\tag{17}
\]
Indeed, among \(1,\dots,mp/2\) there are \(mp/2\) integers in total and exactly \(m/2\) multiples of \(p\). Their difference is
\[
mp/2-m/2=m(p/2),
\]
where all divisions are integer floors; the equality follows by writing each odd number as twice its floor-half plus one.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Full-block relations for even arguments
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Suppose integers \(m,c\ge0\) satisfy
\[
mp=cP.
\tag{18}
\]
Let \(z=U(P)^c\) in \(R\). By (10), for every \(k\ge0\),
\[
U(kmp)=U((kc)P)=z^k.
\tag{19}
\]
It follows immediately that
\[
U(18mp)U(4mp)U(3mp)
=U(9mp)U(8mp)U(6mp)U(2mp)
\pmod{P^3},
\tag{20}
\]
because both sides equal \(z^{25}\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Full- and half-block relations for odd arguments
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Assume now that \(m\) is odd and still that (18) holds. Since \(p\) is odd, all numbers involved in the relevant half-blocks are odd. Define in \(R\)
\[
D=3m(p/2),\quad L=16^D,\quad s=(-1)^D,
\]
\[
A=U(9mp/2+1),\qquad C=U(3mp/2+1),
\]
and retain \(z=U(P)^c\).

Apply the half-block identity (12) first to \(N=9mp=(9c)P\). By (17), the cardinality in that identity is
\[
9m(p/2)=3D.
\]
Using (19), we obtain
\[
A^2L^3=s z^9.
\tag{21}
\]
Here \((-1)^{3D}=(-1)^D=s\). Applying (12) to \(N=3mp=(3c)P\), whose lower-half cardinality is \(3m(p/2)=D\), gives
\[
C^2L=s z^3.
\tag{22}
\]
Equations (21) and (22) imply
\[
(LAz^2)^2=(Cz^5)^2.
\tag{23}
\]
For example, after multiplying both sides by the unit \(L\), the left side becomes
\[
z^4(A^2L^3)=s z^{13},
\]
and the right side becomes
\[
z^{10}(C^2L)=s z^{13}.
\]
Thus the two desired expressions have equal squares. It remains to determine the sign.

We do this modulo \(p\). First, Fermat's theorem gives
\[
2^{p-1}=1\pmod p.
\]
As \(p\) is odd,
\[
16^{p/2}=2^{4(p/2)}=(2^{p-1})^2=1\pmod p.
\tag{24}
\]
Therefore \(L=16^{3m(p/2)}=1\pmod p\).

Let
\[
b=U(p),\qquad h=U(p/2+1)
\]
modulo \(p\). For every odd \(q\), splitting the interval at \((q/2)p\) and using periodicity modulo \(p\) gives
\[
U(qp/2+1)=b^{q/2}h\pmod p.
\tag{25}
\]
Also, by (11), \(U(kmp)=b^{km}\pmod p\). Substituting (25) for \(q=9m\) and \(q=3m\), and collecting powers of \(b\), yields
\[
L\,A\,U(2mp)=C\,U(4mp)\,U(mp)\pmod p.
\tag{26}
\]
Explicitly, after suppressing \(L=1\), the left side is
\[
b^{9m/2}h\,b^{2m}=b^{9m/2+2m}h,
\]
and the right side is
\[
b^{3m/2}h\,b^{4m}b^m=b^{3m/2+5m}h;
\]
the exponents are equal because
\[
9m/2+2m=3m/2+5m
\]
for odd \(m\), with floor division understood.

Now set
\[
X=L A U(2mp)=LAz^2,
\qquad
Y=C U(4mp)U(mp)=Cz^5.
\]
Equation (23) says \(X^2=Y^2\) modulo \(P^3\), while (26) says \(X=Y\) modulo \(p\). Also \(Y\) is a unit because it is a product of \(p\)-free blocks. Hence \(X+Y\), reduced modulo \(p\), equals \(2Y\), which is a unit since \(p\ge5\). An element modulo \(P^3\) whose reduction modulo \(p\) is a unit is itself a unit. Therefore \(X+Y\) is invertible modulo \(P^3\). From
\[
0=X^2-Y^2=(X-Y)(X+Y)
\]
we may cancel \(X+Y\), obtaining \(X=Y\). Thus
\[
16^{3m(p/2)}U(9mp/2+1)U(2mp)
=U(3mp/2+1)U(4mp)U(mp)
\pmod{P^3}.
\tag{27}
\]
This is the required odd block relation.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. Removing the powers of \(p\) from factorials
--------------------------------------------------------------------

For all \(n\ge0\), separating the multiples of \(p\) from the factors of \(n!\) gives the exact identity
\[
n!=p^{\lfloor n/p\rfloor}\lfloor n/p\rfloor!\,U(n+1).
\tag{28}
\]
Indeed, the factors divisible by \(p\) are \(p,2p,\dots,\lfloor n/p\rfloor p\), whose product is the first two factors on the right, and all remaining factors make up \(U(n+1)\).

Two useful special cases are
\[
(mp)!=p^m m!\,U(mp)
\tag{29}
\]
and
\[
(mp/2)!=p^{m/2}(m/2)!\,U(mp/2+1).
\tag{30}
\]
In (29), \(U(mp+1)=U(mp)\) because the added endpoint \(mp\) is divisible by \(p\). Formula (30) follows from
\(\lfloor (mp/2)/p\rfloor=\lfloor m/2\rfloor\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Rewriting the Gamma quotient according to parity
--------------------------------------------------------------------

For even arguments, the Gamma factors are all ordinary factorials. Directly from \(\Gamma(k+1)=k!\),
\[
a(2m)=
\frac{(18m)!(4m)!(3m)!}
{(9m)!(8m)!(6m)!(2m)!}.
\tag{31}
\]

For odd arguments, use the Gamma duplication formula
\[
\Gamma(x)\Gamma(x+1/2)=2^{1-2x}\sqrt\pi\,\Gamma(2x).
\]
Applied with \(x=(k+1)/2\), it gives, for every nonnegative integer \(k\),
\[
\Gamma((k+1)/2)\Gamma(k/2+1)2^k=k!\sqrt\pi.
\tag{32}
\]
When \(n\) is odd, apply (32) to \(k=9n\) and \(k=3n\). The two factors \(\sqrt\pi\) cancel in the quotient defining \(a(n)\), and the remaining integral Gamma factors become factorials. The result is
\[
a(n)=2^{6n}
\frac{(9n/2)!(2n)!}
{(3n/2)!(4n)!n!},
\qquad n\text{ odd},
\tag{33}
\]
where the divisions in the factorial indices are floors.

We next derive exact transfer identities over the real numbers.

From (31), applying (29) to every factorial in \(a(2mp)\) and cancelling all powers of \(p\) and all smaller factorials gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(2mp)&\,U(9mp)U(8mp)U(6mp)U(2mp)\\
&=a(2m)\,U(18mp)U(4mp)U(3mp).
\end{aligned}
\tag{34}
\]
The cancellation is exact: the numerator exponents of the common quantity \(p^m\) are \(18+4+3=25\), as are the denominator exponents \(9+8+6+2=25\).

For odd \(m\), formulas (29), (30), and (33) similarly give
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(mp)&\,U(3mp/2+1)U(4mp)U(mp)\\
&=a(m)\,16^{3m(p/2)}U(9mp/2+1)U(2mp).
\end{aligned}
\tag{35}
\]
Here the extra power of \(16\) comes from the exact identity
\[
2^{6mp}=2^{6m}16^{3m(p/2)},
\tag{36}
\]
valid because \(p=2(p/2)+1\). The powers of \(p\) introduced by stripping the factorials also cancel: one uses
\[
9m/2=3m/2+3m.
\]
Thus (34) and (35) are identities of real numbers, not merely congruences.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7. One-step congruences for integral values
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Assume the two values in (34) are integers, say
\[
A=a(2mp),\qquad B=a(2m).
\]
Then (34), being an equality between integers viewed as real numbers, is an integer equality. Reduce it modulo \(P^3\). By the even block relation (20), the block product multiplying \(A\) equals the block product multiplying \(B\). This common product is a unit modulo \(P^3\), since none of its factors is divisible by \(p\). Cancelling it gives
\[
a(2mp)\equiv a(2m)\pmod{P^3}
\tag{37}
\]
whenever \(mp=cP\).

Likewise, if \(m\) is odd and \(a(mp),a(m)\) are integers, reduce (35) modulo \(P^3\). The odd block relation (27) identifies the two block products, and that common product is again a unit. Cancellation gives
\[
a(mp)\equiv a(m)\pmod{P^3}
\tag{38}
\]
whenever \(m\) is odd and \(mp=cP\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
8. Completion of the supercongruence
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Let \(n,r>0\), and retain \(P=p^r\). We compare \(a(np^r)\) and \(a(np^{r-1})\).

If \(n\) is even, put
\[
m=(n/2)p^{r-1},\qquad c=n/2.
\]
Then
\[
mp=(n/2)p^r=cP,
\]
and
\[
2mp=np^r,\qquad 2m=np^{r-1}.
\]
Applying (37) gives
\[
a(np^r)\equiv a(np^{r-1})\pmod{P^3}.
\]

If \(n\) is odd, put
\[
m=np^{r-1},\qquad c=n.
\]
Both \(n\) and \(p\) are odd, so \(m\) is odd. Moreover,
\[
mp=np^r=cP.
\]
Applying (38) again gives
\[
a(np^r)\equiv a(np^{r-1})\pmod{P^3}.
\]

Finally,
\[
P^3=(p^r)^3=p^{3r}.
\]
Thus in both parity cases
\[
\boxed{\ a(np^r)\equiv a(np^{r-1})\pmod{p^{3r}}\ }.
\]
Because the integrality hypothesis identifies each real value \(a(k)\) with a unique integer, this is precisely the claimed congruence for the chosen integer representatives of the sequence values.
